guides.title: Psalms: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A song can move without erasing its beginning
steps.text: The first line accuses and still says “my God” twice. The speaker complains to the one he feels has left. The poem then swings between pain and memory. Complaint and memory alternate through verses 1–10. From verse 22 it becomes praise. Verse 24 says God has not hidden his face. Jesus speaks the first line on the cross in Mark 15:34.

steps.title: Some prayers end without visible relief
steps.text: This is the one prayer in the book with no turn toward hope. Its last word is “darkness.” Yet verse 1 calls the LORD “the God of my salvation.” The speaker says three times that he keeps praying (verses 1, 9, 13). His faith shows in the fact that he still speaks. The book of Psalms includes this prayer with the rest. A person may pray this way and still be praying.

steps.title: Exile changes what a song can do
steps.text: The captors request music from people who have lost their home. They want Zion’s worship as entertainment. Verse 4 links the LORD’s song with a place and with freedom. The final anger in verses 8–9 must be read beside that loss. Second Kings 25:7 shows what these people had seen. A Babylonian hymn tablet provides a comparison with another tradition of sacred songs. It does not prove that this psalm borrowed from that hymn.

steps.title: Praise includes bodies, skills, and many sounds
steps.text: The poem answers four questions in order. Verse 1 says where, and verse 2 says why. Verses 3–5 say how, and verse 6 says who. Verses 3–5 name trumpet, strings, drums, dancing, flute, and cymbals. An Egyptian harp shows one ancient form of a string instrument. Praise uses breath, hands, skill, and the whole body. The book began with one blessed person and ends with everything that breathes.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: This short poem opens the book of Psalms. It calls a person blessed who stays away from the advice of the wicked. That person delights in the LORD’s teaching and thinks on it day and night. He is like a tree planted beside streams. The wicked are like chaff that the wind blows away. They will not stand in the judgment. The LORD knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the wicked ends.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: Nations and kings plot against the LORD and his anointed king. The one enthroned in heaven laughs at them. He says he has set his king on Zion, his holy hill. The king reports God’s decree: “You are my son.” The nations are promised to him as an inheritance. The poem then warns the kings of the earth to be wise. They should serve the LORD with fear. All who take refuge in him are blessed.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The heading sets this prayer in David’s flight from his son Absalom. The speaker says his enemies are many. Many say God will not help him. He answers that the LORD is a shield around him. He cried out, and the LORD answered from his holy hill. He lay down, slept, and woke again. He will not fear ten thousand people set against him. He asks the LORD to rise and save.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker asks God to answer when he calls. He asks people how long they will love empty things and lies. He says the LORD has set apart the faithful for himself. He tells them to tremble, search their hearts in bed, and be still. Many ask who will show them any good. The speaker asks for the light of God’s face. He has more joy than others have at harvest. He lies down and sleeps in peace.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker asks the LORD to hear his words and his sighing. He prays in the morning and watches for an answer. God takes no pleasure in wickedness, and the proud cannot stand before him. The LORD hates liars and violent men. The speaker will enter God’s house through great kindness. He asks to be led on a straight path because of his enemies. Their throats are open graves. He asks that all who take refuge in God may rejoice.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker asks the LORD not to rebuke him in anger. He is faint, and his bones are troubled. He asks how long and cannot finish the sentence. He asks to be saved for the sake of God’s kindness. No one praises God from the grave. He floods his bed with tears every night. Then he orders the evildoers to leave. The LORD has heard the sound of his weeping.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The heading says David sang this about the words of Cush the Benjamite. The speaker takes refuge in the LORD from pursuers who tear like a lion. He swears that if he has wronged a friend, his enemy may crush him. He asks the LORD to rise and judge the peoples. He asks to be judged by his own right conduct. God tests hearts and minds. The one who digs a pit falls into it. The speaker gives thanks for the LORD’s justice.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The poem begins and ends by praising the LORD’s majestic name. His glory is above the heavens. Even the mouths of infants serve as his strength. The speaker looks at the moon and the stars. He asks what a human being is that God should care. Yet God made humans a little lower than the heavenly beings. He crowned them with glory and honor. He put flocks, wild animals, birds, and fish under their care.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker thanks the LORD with his whole heart. His enemies fell back when God judged from the throne. The LORD rules forever and judges the world rightly. He is a high tower for the oppressed. He does not forget the cry of the afflicted. The speaker asks to be lifted from the gates of death. Nations sink in the pit they dug. He asks God to let the nations know they are only human.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker asks why the LORD stands far off in times of trouble. A proud man hunts the poor. He says in his heart that there is no God to call him to account. His ways prosper, and he thinks nothing can shake him. He waits in ambush in the villages and seizes the helpless. The speaker asks God to rise and lift his hand. He says God does see trouble and grief. The LORD hears the humble and defends the orphan.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker has taken refuge in the LORD. Friends tell him to flee like a bird to the mountains. The wicked have bent their bows to shoot from the dark. If the foundations are destroyed, they ask, what can the righteous do? The speaker answers that the LORD is in his holy temple. His throne is in heaven, and his eyes examine everyone. He tests the righteous and hates violence. The upright will see his face.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker cries for help because faithful people have vanished. Everyone lies to his neighbor with flattering lips. The proud say their tongues will win and no one rules them. The LORD answers that he will now rise. He acts because the weak are oppressed and the needy groan. The LORD’s words are pure, like silver refined seven times. He will guard the poor. Still the wicked strut about when vileness is honored.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker asks the LORD four times, “How long?” He asks whether God will forget him forever. He has sorrow in his heart every day. His enemy is winning. He asks God to look, answer, and give light to his eyes. Otherwise he will sleep in death. Then he says he trusts in God’s kindness. He will sing, because the LORD has been good to him.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The fool says in his heart that there is no God. People are corrupt, and no one does good. The LORD looks down from heaven to see whether anyone seeks him. All have turned aside. Evildoers eat up God’s people as they eat bread. They do not call on the LORD. Yet God is with the righteous, and he is the refuge of the poor. There he understood their end. He says God holds his hand and is his portion forever.

Brave soldiers lay stunned, and at his rebuke horse and chariot fell still. No one can stand when he is angry. The earth feared and was quiet when God rose to judge. He rose to save all the afflicted of the earth. Rulers should bring gifts to the one who humbles princes.

He asks whether the Lord will reject forever and whether his kindness has ended. Then he decides to remember the LORD’s deeds of old. God redeemed the children of Jacob and Joseph. The waters saw him and trembled. He led his people through the sea like a flock.

He recalls the sea, the cloud, water from the rock, and manna. The people still tested God and forgot his works. God was merciful and remembered that they were only flesh. He left Shiloh and let the ark be captured. He chose Judah, Mount Zion, and David the shepherd.

Neighbors mock the survivors. The people ask how long God will be angry. They ask him not to hold their earlier sins against them. They ask for help and forgiveness for the sake of his name. Then his people, his flock, will thank him forever.

He has fed them with tears. They recall that God brought a vine out of Egypt and planted it. It filled the land and shaded the mountains. Now its walls are broken, passersby pick its fruit, and a wild boar tears it. They ask God to look down and care for this vine.

He lifted the burden from Israel’s shoulder in Egypt. He tells his people to have no foreign god. He brought them out of Egypt and will fill their open mouths. But the people would not listen, so he let them follow their own plans. If they would listen, he would feed them with the finest wheat.

The poet asks God to rise and judge the earth, since all nations are his.

Ten peoples have joined together, from Edom and Moab to Tyre and Assyria. The people ask God to treat them as he treated Midian and Sisera. They ask that the enemies be like windblown dust and their faces filled with shame. Then they may seek his name. Let them know that the LORD alone is Most High.

So are those who set their hearts on the road to Zion. They pass through a dry valley and make it a place of springs. A day in God’s courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. The speaker would choose to be a doorkeeper there. The LORD is a sun and shield.

The speaker will listen for what God says. God speaks peace to his people, and they must not return to folly. Mercy and truth meet. Righteousness and peace kiss each other. The LORD will give what is good, and the land will yield its harvest.

All nations he made will come and worship. The speaker asks to be taught God’s way. He asks for an undivided heart. Proud and violent men seek his life. He calls God merciful and gracious and asks for a sign of favor.

Of each one it is said, “This one was born there.” The Most High himself will establish Zion. When he registers the peoples, he records them as born in her. Singers and dancers say all their springs are in her.

He is counted among the dead whom God remembers no more. God’s anger lies heavy on him. He asks whether God works wonders for the dead. He has been afflicted since his youth. Friend and neighbor are gone, and darkness is his companion.

chapterMaps.narrative: The heading names Ethan the Ezrahite. The poet sings of the LORD’s kindness and faithfulness. God swore that David’s line and throne would last forever. The heavens praise him, and justice is the base of his throne. If David’s sons sin, God will punish them and still keep his kindness. Then the poem turns. God has rejected his anointed and thrown the crown in the dust. Walls are broken, enemies rejoice, and the poet asks where the former kindness is.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.narrative: The heading calls this a prayer of Moses. The Lord has been his people’s home in every generation. He was God before the mountains were born. A thousand years are like a day to him. People are like grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening. A life lasts seventy or eighty years and is full of toil. The speaker asks God to teach them to count their days. He asks God to establish the work of their hands.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The poem speaks of one who lives in the shelter of the Most High. God will save him from the hunter’s trap and from deadly disease. He covers him with his feathers. He need not fear terror by night or arrows by day. Angels will guard him and lift him up. Then God speaks. He will rescue the one who loves him and answer when he calls. He will be with him in trouble and give him long life.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.narrative: The heading calls this a song for the Sabbath day. It is good to thank the LORD with harp and lyre. His works make the speaker glad, and his thoughts are deep. A senseless person does not understand this. The wicked sprout like grass and are destroyed forever. The righteous flourish like a palm and grow like a cedar. They are planted in the LORD’s house. They still bear fruit in old age.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD reigns and is robed in majesty. He has made the world firm, and it cannot be moved. His throne was set up long ago. The floods have lifted up their voice and their pounding waves. The LORD on high is mightier than the thunder of many waters. His decrees are very sure. Holiness belongs to his house forever.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker calls on God to rise as judge of the earth. The wicked crush God’s people. They kill the widow, the foreigner, and the orphan. They say the LORD does not see. The speaker answers that the maker of the ear can hear. The LORD will not abandon his people. When the speaker’s foot slipped, God’s kindness held him up. He asks whether a wicked throne that makes harm legal can be God’s ally.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

They are called to kneel before their Maker. They are the sheep of his hand. Then a warning comes: hear his voice today. Do not harden your hearts as at Meribah in the wilderness. That generation tested God and did not enter his rest.

Families of nations should bring him an offering. They should say that the LORD reigns and judges fairly. The heavens, the earth, and the sea are called to rejoice. The fields and the trees of the forest sing. He is coming to judge the earth with justice.

The heavens declare his justice. All who worship idols are put to shame. Those who love the LORD must hate evil. Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the honest in heart.

chapterMaps.narrative: The poem calls for a new song, since the LORD has done wonderful things. His right hand has won the victory. He has shown his saving power to the nations. He remembered his kindness to Israel. All the earth should shout with lyre, trumpets, and horn. The sea should roar, and the rivers clap their hands. The mountains should sing together. The LORD is coming to judge the world fairly.

Moses, Aaron, and Samuel called on him, and he answered. He spoke to them from the pillar of cloud. He forgave them, and he also punished their wrongs. The people are called to worship at his holy hill.

He made them, and they are his. They are his people and the sheep of his pasture. They should enter his gates with thanks and his courts with praise. The LORD is good. His kindness lasts forever, and his faithfulness reaches every generation.

chapterMaps.narrative: A ruler sings of kindness and justice. He promises to live with a blameless heart inside his own house. He will set nothing worthless before his eyes. He will silence anyone who slanders a neighbor in secret. He will not put up with proud looks. He will look for faithful people to live with him and serve him. No liar will stay in his house. Each morning he will remove the wicked from the LORD’s city.

chapterMaps.narrative: The heading calls this the prayer of a suffering person who is faint. His days vanish like smoke, and his heart is withered like grass. He is like a lonely bird on a roof. His enemies mock him, and he eats ashes with his bread. Yet the LORD sits enthroned forever. He will rise and have mercy on Zion. This will be written for a generation still to come. The heavens will wear out like clothing, but God stays the same.

chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker tells his soul to bless the LORD and forget none of his gifts. God forgives, heals, and rescues his life from the pit. He is merciful and gracious and slow to anger. He does not treat people as their sins deserve. His kindness is as high as the heavens are above the earth. He pities his children as a father does. He remembers that people are dust. Human life is like grass, but his kindness lasts forever.

chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker blesses the LORD, who is clothed with light. God stretched out the heavens and set the earth on its foundations. He sends springs into the valleys for the wild animals. He grows grass for cattle and plants, wine, oil, and bread for people. Lions hunt at night, and people work by day. The sea holds creatures beyond number. All of them wait for God to give their food. He takes their breath, and they die; he sends his Spirit, and they are created.

chapterMaps.narrative: The poem calls the people to remember the LORD’s wonders. He made a covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and promised them a land. When they were few, he protected them. He sent Joseph ahead as a slave, and Joseph rose to rule Egypt. Israel grew there and was hated. God sent Moses, Aaron, and the plagues. He brought his people out with joy and fed them in the desert. He gave them lands so that they would keep his laws.

chapterMaps.narrative: The poem begins with praise and a prayer to be remembered. Then it confesses: we have sinned as our fathers did. The fathers forgot God’s wonders at the Red Sea. They craved food in the desert and envied Moses. They made a calf at Horeb, and Moses stood in the gap for them. They joined in the worship of Baal and later sacrificed their children. God gave them over to the nations many times. Yet he heard their cry and remembered his covenant.

chapterMaps.narrative: The poem calls the redeemed to thank the LORD. It describes four groups in trouble. Some wandered hungry in the desert. Some sat in dark prisons because they had rebelled. Some were sick through their own folly. Some were caught in a storm at sea. Each group cried to the LORD, and he rescued them. He turns rivers into desert and desert into pools, and the wise will consider this.

chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker’s heart is steady, and he will sing and wake the dawn. He will give thanks among the nations. God’s kindness is higher than the heavens. He asks God to save with his right hand. God has spoken: Shechem, Gilead, Ephraim, and Judah are his. Moab, Edom, and Philistia are under him. Yet God has not gone out with their armies. With God they will still do bravely.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker asks God not to stay silent. Liars surround him and attack him without cause. They repay his love with accusation, and he prays. A long series of curses follows. The accused man should lose his office, his family, and his name. He never showed kindness and hunted the poor to death. The speaker is poor, weak from fasting, and mocked. He asks God to save him, for God stands beside the needy.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells the speaker’s lord to sit at his right hand. His enemies will become his footstool. The LORD will extend his rule from Zion. His people offer themselves freely on the day of battle. The LORD has sworn an oath and will not change it. This ruler is a priest forever, like Melchizedek. The Lord at his right hand will shatter kings. He will judge the nations and lift up his head.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker will thank the LORD with his whole heart among the upright. The LORD’s works are great and are studied by all who enjoy them. He is gracious and merciful. He gives food to those who fear him and remembers his covenant. He gave his people the lands of other nations. His commands are trustworthy and lasting. He sent redemption to his people. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.narrative: The poem blesses the person who fears the LORD and delights in his commands. His children will be strong, and his house will have wealth. Light rises in the dark for the upright. He is gracious, lends freely, and runs his affairs justly. He will not be shaken or fear bad news. His heart is steady. He gives freely to the poor. The wicked see it, are angry, and melt away.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

He stoops to look at the heavens and the earth. He raises the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap. He seats them with princes. He gives the childless woman a home and makes her a joyful mother.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel went out of Egypt, from a people of foreign speech. Judah became God’s sanctuary. The sea saw it and fled, and the Jordan turned back. The mountains skipped like rams and the hills like lambs. The poet asks the sea and the river why they ran. He asks the mountains why they skipped. The earth should tremble before the God of Jacob. He turned the rock into a pool of water.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.narrative: The people ask that glory go to the LORD’s name and not to them. The nations ask where their God is. He is in the heavens and does whatever he pleases. The nations’ idols are silver and gold, made by human hands. They have mouths, eyes, ears, and hands that do nothing. Those who make them will become like them. Israel should trust the LORD, their help and shield. He will bless those who fear him, small and great.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker loves the LORD, who heard his cry. The cords of death had wrapped around him. He called on the LORD’s name and was saved. God rescued his life from death, his eyes from tears, and his feet from falling. He asks what he can give back to the LORD. He will lift the cup of salvation and call on the LORD’s name. He will keep his vows before all the people. He will offer thanks in the courts of the LORD’s house.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.narrative: This is the shortest psalm. It calls all nations to praise the LORD. It calls all peoples to honor him. The reason is that his kindness toward us is great. His faithfulness lasts forever.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.narrative: The people give thanks, for the LORD’s kindness lasts forever. The speaker called in distress, and the LORD set him free. Nations surrounded him like bees, and he cut them off in the LORD’s name. He was pushed hard and nearly fell. He will not die but live and tell what the LORD has done. He asks for the gates to be opened. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The people bless the one who comes in the LORD’s name.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.narrative: This is the longest psalm. It has twenty-two sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Almost every verse names God’s teaching as law, word, statute, or command. The speaker is young and feels like a stranger on the earth. Princes slander him, and he has suffered. He says God’s word is a lamp for his feet. He loves the commands more than gold. He ends by saying he has strayed like a lost sheep.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: This is the first of fifteen songs of ascents. The speaker cried to the LORD in distress and was answered. He asks to be saved from lying lips. He asks what a deceitful tongue deserves: sharp arrows and burning coals. He grieves that he lives in Meshech and among the tents of Kedar. He has lived too long with people who hate peace. He is for peace. When he speaks, they are for war.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker lifts his eyes to the hills and asks where his help comes from. It comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth. God will not let his foot slip. The one who keeps Israel does not slumber or sleep. The LORD is his keeper and his shade. The sun will not harm him by day or the moon by night. The LORD will keep him from all evil. He will guard his going out and coming in forever.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker was glad when people said, “Let’s go to the LORD’s house.” Now his feet stand inside Jerusalem’s gates. The city is built firmly together. The tribes go up there to give thanks to the LORD. Thrones for judgment stand there, the thrones of David’s house. He calls for prayer for Jerusalem’s peace. He wishes peace within its walls. He seeks its good for the sake of his family and the LORD’s house.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker lifts his eyes to the one enthroned in heaven. Servants watch the hand of their master. A maid watches the hand of her mistress. In the same way the people watch the LORD until he shows mercy. They ask for mercy twice. They have had more than enough contempt. They are worn out by the scorn of the comfortable and the proud.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The people say what would have happened without the LORD on their side. When men attacked, they would have been swallowed alive. The flood would have swept over them. The raging waters would have gone over their heads. They bless the LORD, who did not give them to those teeth. They escaped like a bird from a hunter’s trap. The trap broke. Their help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.narrative: Those who trust the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved. Mountains surround Jerusalem. In the same way the LORD surrounds his people now and forever. Wicked rule will not stay over the land of the righteous. Otherwise the righteous might turn to doing wrong. The poet asks the LORD to do good to the good. Those who turn to crooked ways will be led away. Peace be on Israel.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: When the LORD brought back Zion’s captives, the people were like dreamers. Their mouths were full of laughter and song. The nations said the LORD had done great things for them. The people agree and are glad. They ask the LORD to restore them again like streams in the Negev. Those who sow in tears will reap with joy. The one who goes out weeping with seed will return with sheaves.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders work for nothing. Unless the LORD guards the city, the guard stays awake for nothing. It is useless to rise early and stay up late in anxious toil. God gives sleep to those he loves. Children are a gift from the LORD. They are like arrows in a warrior’s hand. The man with many is blessed. They will stand with him against enemies at the gate.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: Everyone who fears the LORD and walks in his ways is blessed. He will eat what his own hands have worked for. His wife will be like a fruitful vine in his house. His children will be like olive shoots around his table. The poem asks the LORD to bless him from Zion. May he see Jerusalem’s good all his life. May he see his children’s children. Peace be on Israel.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: Israel says it has been attacked many times since its youth. Yet its enemies have not won. Plowmen plowed its back and made their furrows long. The LORD is just and has cut the cords of the wicked. May all who hate Zion be turned back. May they be like grass on a roof that withers before it grows. No reaper fills his hands with it. No passerby gives it a blessing.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker cries to the LORD out of the depths. He asks the Lord to hear his voice. If God kept a record of sins, no one could stand. But with God there is forgiveness. The speaker waits for the LORD and hopes in his word. He waits more than watchmen wait for the morning. He tells Israel to hope in the LORD. With him is kindness and full redemption.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker tells the LORD that his heart is not proud. His eyes are not raised too high. He does not busy himself with matters too great for him. He has calmed and quieted his soul. His soul is like a weaned child with its mother. He tells Israel to hope in the LORD now and forever.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The poem asks the LORD to remember David and his hardships. David swore not to rest until he found a place for the LORD. The people heard of the ark and went to worship at his footstool. They ask the LORD to arise and come to his resting place. The LORD swore that David’s sons would sit on his throne. The LORD has chosen Zion for his home. He will bless her food and satisfy her poor with bread. He will make David’s strength grow there.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The poem says how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity. It is like fine oil poured on the head. The oil runs down Aaron’s beard to the collar of his robes. It is like the dew of Mount Hermon falling on the hills of Zion. There the LORD commands his blessing. That blessing is life forever.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: This is the last of the songs of ascents. It calls the LORD’s servants to bless him. They stand in the LORD’s house by night. They are told to lift their hands toward the holy place. Then a blessing is spoken in return. May the LORD, who made heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The poem calls the LORD’s servants to praise his name. He chose Jacob for himself. He does whatever he pleases in heaven, earth, and sea. He brings clouds, lightning, and wind. He struck Egypt’s firstborn and defeated great kings. He gave their land to Israel. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by hands. Israel, Aaron’s house, and Levi’s house are called to bless the LORD.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The poem calls the people to thank the LORD, for he is good. Every line ends with “for his loving kindness endures forever.” He alone does great wonders. He made the heavens, the earth, the sun, and the moon. He brought Israel out of Egypt and divided the Red Sea. He led his people through the desert and struck down kings. He remembered them when they were low. He gives food to every creature.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The exiles sat by the rivers of Babylon and wept for Zion. They hung their harps on the trees. Their captors asked them for a song of Zion. They ask how they can sing the LORD’s song in a foreign land. The speaker swears never to forget Jerusalem. He asks the LORD to remember what Edom said when the city fell. He speaks of Babylon’s coming ruin. The poem ends with fierce words about repayment.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker thanks the LORD with his whole heart. He sings praise before the “gods” and bows toward the holy temple. On the day he called, God answered and gave him strength. All the kings of the earth will thank the LORD. The LORD is high, yet he looks after the lowly. He knows the proud from far away. He keeps the speaker alive in trouble. The speaker asks him not to abandon the work of his hands.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD has searched the speaker and knows him. He knows when he sits and rises and what he will say. The speaker cannot flee from God’s Spirit. In heaven, in the grave, or across the sea, God’s hand holds him. Darkness is as light to God. God formed him in his mother’s womb. All his days were written before one of them came. He asks God to search his heart and lead him.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker asks the LORD to rescue him from evil and violent men. They plan harm and stir up strife all day. Their tongues are sharp like a serpent’s. The proud have hidden traps and nets for him. He says the LORD is his God and covers his head in battle. He asks that their own words bring them down. He knows the LORD upholds the cause of the poor. The upright will live in God’s presence.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker calls on the LORD to come quickly. He asks that his prayer rise like incense. He asks God to set a guard over his mouth. He asks that his heart not lean toward evil. He does not want to share the feasts of wrongdoers. He would welcome a good person’s rebuke as a kindness. His eyes are fixed on the LORD. He asks to be kept from the traps set for him.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The heading sets this prayer in the cave where David hid. The speaker cries aloud and pours out his complaint. When his spirit is faint, God knows his path. Enemies have hidden a trap on the road. He looks to his right, and no one is there. No one cares about his life. He cries that the LORD is his refuge. He asks to be brought out of prison, and the righteous will gather around him.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker asks the LORD to hear him and answer in faithfulness. He asks God not to bring him to judgment. No one living is righteous before God. An enemy has crushed his life and made him sit in darkness. He remembers the days of old and stretches out his hands. His soul thirsts like dry ground. He asks to hear of God’s kindness in the morning. He asks to be taught the way to go.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker blesses the LORD, his rock, who trains his hands for battle. He asks what a human is, a breath and a passing shadow. He asks God to bend the heavens and come down. He asks rescue from foreigners whose mouths speak lies. He will sing a new song on the ten-stringed lyre. Then sons will grow like strong plants and daughters like carved pillars. Barns will be full and flocks many. No cry of distress will be heard in the streets.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker will praise God his King every day. One generation will tell the next of God’s mighty acts. The LORD is gracious, merciful, and slow to anger. He is good to all. His kingdom lasts through all generations. He holds up all who fall. Every creature looks to him for food at the right time. He is near to all who call on him in truth.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The speaker will praise the LORD as long as he lives. He warns against trusting in princes. A human ruler dies, and his plans die that day. The one whose help is the God of Jacob is blessed. God made heaven, earth, and sea and keeps faith forever. He gives justice to the oppressed and food to the hungry. He frees prisoners and opens blind eyes. He guards foreigners, orphans, and widows.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: It is good to sing praise to the LORD. He builds up Jerusalem and gathers Israel’s outcasts. He heals the brokenhearted and binds their wounds. He counts the stars and names each one. He covers the sky with clouds and feeds animals and young ravens. He takes no pleasure in a horse’s strength. He sends snow, frost, and hail, and his word melts them. He has given his word to Israel.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The poem calls for praise from the heavens. Angels, sun, moon, and stars are told to praise the LORD. He commanded, and they were created. Then it calls for praise from the earth. Sea creatures, fire, hail, snow, and wind are named. Mountains, trees, wild animals, cattle, and birds follow. Kings and all peoples are called, young and old. The LORD’s name alone is exalted.
chapterMaps.limits: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

chapterMaps.note: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.
chapterMaps.narrative: The poem calls for a new song in the gathering of the faithful. Israel should rejoice in its Maker. The people praise with dancing, tambourine, and lyre. The LORD takes pleasure in his people and honors the humble with victory. The faithful sing for joy on their beds. Praise is in their mouths and a two-edged sword in their hands. They are to carry out the judgment that is written. This is the honor of all his faithful ones.
chapterMaps.limits: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapterMaps.note: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: The last psalm calls for praise to God in his sanctuary and in the heavens. He is to be praised for his mighty acts and his greatness. Praise him with trumpet, harp, and lyre. Praise him with tambourine and dancing. Praise him with strings, pipe, and loud cymbals. Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.
